Cartesian Coordinates

CoordinatesAlgebra
Game: A set of axes lets you name any spot on a flat board with two numbers; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Move the pointer over the board to read a spot. Drag the red dot in the middle to move the axes, and the other red dot to stretch them.

Keyboard: focus the board, press O (origin), U (unit point) or C (cursor), then the arrow keys.

Look for the math

Two number lines at right angles turn every point of a plane into a pair of numbers, and every pair into a point. That is the idea of Cartesian coordinates.

Reading a point

Draw a line through the point parallel to each axis. Where they meet the axes gives the x-coordinate (the abscissa) and the y-coordinate (the ordinate). In pixels, a point at (px, py) reads x = (px − ox) / unit and y = (oy − py) / unit, rounded to the nearest whole number as the applet does. The logic test checked that every lattice point reads back as itself and that every pixel reads its nearest lattice point.

Distance

By the Pythagorean theorem, the distance from the origin to (x, y) is √(x² + y²), and between two points √((x₁ − x₂)² + (y₁ − y₂)²). Change the unit and every pixel distance is scaled by it, but the numbers stay the same.

Complex form

Write the point (x, y) as x + yi and it becomes a complex number, with distance from the origin |x + yi| = √(x² + y²), its modulus. The applet drops a zero real part and a coefficient of 1 (so you see +i, not 0 + 1i); it also leaves no space after the sign of the imaginary part, which this page keeps.

Choose complex form, trace the cursor, and move to (0, 1): the applet reads it as +i. Then drag the unit point to make the units tiny and watch the same numbers cover more of the board.
